entries.title: From the Archive: “The Loves of Lena Dunham”
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
In this episode of Private Life, the actress and comedian Ruby McCollister reads Elaine Blair’s essay “The Loves of Lena Dunham,” about the HBO series Girls and its depictions of sex, from the Review’s June 7, 2012, issue.

McCollister can be seen in Maddie’s Secret (2025), The French Italian (2024), Search Party (2016–2022), and Curb Your Enthusiasm (2000–2024).

Last week’s episode was an interview with Blair that discussed her essays on feminism and television for the Review.

entries.title: Nose in a Book
entries.summary: A dispatch from the Art Editor
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
I’ve been thinking about physical books lately: the size of what we read versus the size of smartphones; how the US military passed out more than 120 million paperbacks to soldiers during World War II; the history of mass market paperbacks (which aren’t much bigger than smartphones) and who buys hardcovers; and the so-called crisis of reading that I’m both aware of and insulated from here at the Review. I decided to do some extremely unscientific research and count the number of people reading books on the subway. I made a diagram of each car I rode in, making a mark on the seats where a person was reading a physical book. I saw the greatest number of books per car on the G train, which connects Brooklyn to Queens. Most passengers were reading paperbacks, though I did have the odd hardcover sighting. I saw Salinger and Dostoevsky and Suzanne Collins. Most titles I could not make out from where I was sitting or standing.

This newsletter, covering the art and illustrations in the past four issues of the magazine, comes to you from those notes. (The red letters or numbers at the bottom of each diagram indicate which train I was on.)

The cover of the Fall Books Issue was graced with a punnet of plums. I went into detail about the origin of the artwork (cake) and collaboration (happy) between ink-maker Jason Logan and director Lena Beug in this “Brief Encounters” interview.

Inside, the issue opens with a wonderful essay on faith by Meghan O’Gieblyn, excerpted from her book Will and Attention. The accompanying painting is titled El primer cop (2024), by the Barcelona-based artist Guim Tió, whose work often evokes the scale of nature with figures set against vast landscapes. Michelle Mildenberg drew our frequent contributor Nathaniel Rich in front of a data center interior for James Walton’s review of his ripping new heist novel Cloudthief. (Back in July I had the pleasure of interviewing Rich about the book, his preoccupation with fugitivity, and dark utopian caves at Brooklyn’s Community Bookstore.)

The designer and writer Oliver Munday cobbled together a collage for Jacob Weisberg’s essay about how Dartmouth College and its president, Sian Beilock, have worked with the Trump administration. Vivienne Flesher drew the novelist Gwendoline Riley for a review by Miranda Seymour of her latest novel, prompting one editor to ask what was up with the visual trope of “encircled women’s faces,” but the coincidence didn’t bother me.

Joy Williams, one of my favorite writers, reviewed Lance Richardson’s biography of Peter Matthiessen, and Andrea Ventura drew a craggy likeness of the storied nature writer. Richardson later wrote to ask for a print of the illustration.

Our editorial assistant Anika Banister found a wonderful piece of glitchy, samizdat-esque art by Soledad Salamé for Jed Rakoff’s consideration of how federal judges think about climate change, and I found a painting by Greg Burak for Susan Neiman’s thoughts on universal morality. Burak’s paintings often feel as though there is a choice hanging in the balance and indeed he pointed out that his last contribution to the Review was also for a book about morals. I found a dotty body by the French illustrator Jochen Gerner to run with Jerome Groopman’s article on the mysteries of medical diagnosis.

The series art for the issue, titled Studies in Pencil Shavings, was by the London-based illustrator Maria-Ines Gul.

A pair of eyeglasses belonging to Mikhail Gorbachev’s translator appears on the front of the October 8 issue, in a rare photographic cover—we only do one or two a year, if that. The image is from the artist Taryn Simon’s solo show at the Guggenheim, “Father Country I Do Love You”; inside the issue we excerpted some of Simon’s text from the show. This decades-in-the-making body of work follows the career of one anonymous federal agent and the big and small ways his work intersected international events.

For Michael Gorra on the New Orleans novels of Nancy Lemann, I wrote to another photographer, Alec Soth, asking if we might use a daylit composition of a nearly empty room with a midcentury portrait on the wall, which was featured in his 2004 book Sleeping by the Mississippi. Tom Bachtell made a deft double portrait of the sinister twins Donald Trump and Roy Cohn for Fintan O’Toole’s review of a biography of Cohn.

In a strange alignment of art and story, Anahid Nersessian’s review of the book Dad Had a Bad Dayby Ashton Politanoff was matched perfectly by the artist Sara Perović’s 2020 photographic series My Father’s Legs. Both are poignant and funny portraits of the midlife tennis-playing father. I was happy that the great Belgian painter and filmmaker Michaël Borremans let us use his 2020 painting Little Missile to illustrate Jerry Brown’s essay on the continuing threat of nuclear weapons.

Advertisement

John Broadley, who always reads closely, drew Mary and Charles Lamb at their table for Francis Wilson’s review of the fourth volume of the Lambs’ complete works, and when he sent the sketch thoughtfully noted that “the prints on the walls will be simplified drawings of Gin Alley and one of Hermia and Helena—just enough to be recognizable to those who spot them.” John Brooks had drawn Mario Vargas Llosa in 2023, when Larry Rohter reviewed his book Harsh Times, so when it came time to publish Ariel Dorfman’s review of Llosa’s final book, we returned to Brooks.

Despite a heavy workload, Alain Pilon was able to take on a portrait of a fellow Canadian, the poet Lisa Robertson, and James McMullan, always great at depicting performing artists, did a quick and vigorous portrait of the conductor Gustavo Dudamel.

The series art, titled Signatures, is by the Australia-born artist Edwina White.

I looked for images of men for our October 22 cover, given some of the issue’s essays: Gavin Francis on bodybuilding and Alan Hollinghurst on Peter Hujar and Paul Thek. We settled on a 2019 painting by the Australian artist Clara Adolphs, titled Upside Down, that seemed both aerobic and erotic. (Adolphs’s work was also featured on our March 24, 2022, cover, which the fashion designer Rachel Comey put on some of her dress designs.) Inside, the Ottawa-based Mike Haddad illustrated the Francis article with a strongman holding a smartphone, and the cartoonist Adrian Tomine drew the novelist Ali Smith surrounded by ghosts.

I emailed Deng Zi, an illustrator we hadn’t worked with before, for an essay by Howard French on how the Chinese government polices the Internet. He sent a circuit-board version of a traditional Chinese kite. We got a beautiful drawing of Philip Glass by Yann Kebbi for Matthew Aucoin’s essay on the composer’s career and the premiere of his newest orchestral work, Symphony No. 15, Lincoln.

Romy Blümel painted Wilfred Sheed for a Jonathan Lethem consideration of Sheed’s career and the republication of his 1966 novel, Office Politics. For Noah Feldman’s essay on how the Supreme Court has enabled President Trump’s undemocratic course, the photographer and designer Michael Schmelling, inspired by former justice Antonin Scalia’s declaration that the Constitution was “dead, dead, dead,” sent in a coffin-shaped Constitution. Lola Seaton writes about the British novelist Jonathan Buckley and his latest book, which is set on the coast of Greece. I was over budget for the issue, but fortunately, before the pandemic, I had painted some scenes from Hydra, so used one watercolor to illustrate the piece.

The Berlin-based illustrator Sophia Martineck drew the influential philosopher Jürgen Habermas, who died in March, in “his modernist house…where you can see the Starnberg Lake and the mountains through the window.” Martineck is a maestro of lovely details, and my favorite part might be the finger sandwiches she placed on his table.

The series art in the issue, titled Fragments from the Queens of the Luxembourg Garden, is by Victoire Bourgois, who has a show of paintings at Entrance Gallery in New York opening in November.

Our November 5 issue is covered in eyes: the artwork Looks by the Spanish illustrator Guridi. I saw it on his Instagram feed and messaged him to see if we could use it. On page 10 more eyes replace the stars on the American flag in Matt Dorfman’s illustration for Sue Halpern’s essay about Silicon Valley’s attacks on democracy. For Meghan O’Gieblyn’s review of Claire-Louise Bennett’s latest novel Big Kiss, Bye-Bye,the Netherlands-based illustrator Hanneke Rozemuller drew Bennett backgrounded by the letters and emails that pervade her stories.

Julian Gewirtz wrote about the race for AI dominance between the US and China, so I emailed Oliver Munday again. He sent an image of the Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang embedded in a super-chip. The writer James Gleick and his editor Gabriel Winslow-Yost happen to be fans of the Baltimore-based illustrator, designer, and writer George Wylesol, so they were glad when I suggested he illustrate Gleick’s essay about deceitful chatbots. Wylesol drew an appropriately creepy personification of a blank-eyed chatbot. For Daisy Hildyard’s review of Saul Leslie’s first novel, A Working Title I Want to Change, Michelle Mildenberg drew Leslie in front of a soul-numbing workplace backroom.

After the illustrator Carly Blumenthal read Adam Thirlwell’s review of Wallace Shawn’s latest play, she drew the playwright and actor “sitting in a restaurant, as it’s mentioned that many of his characters end up at them. There is an empty table behind him, with a chair facing forward and a warm cup of coffee, in reference to the stage design of What We Did Before Our Moth Days. I also included a Chelsea, NY-like scene behind him through a window. I enjoyed the snippet of the essay where he’s quoted expressing his enthusiasm for a play set in Chelsea and thought it would be a fitting setting for the drawing as well.”

Advertisement

The series art in the issue, by Fien Jorrisen, is titled Fragments of a Village. She made it using techniques of cardboard printing and collagraphy, after taking a printmaking class.

entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
In the fall of 2015 I attended a workshop at our children’s elementary school that warned of the dangers of Snapchat, the social media platform popular, in those days, with tweens and teens. Adults feared that “snaps,” or disappearing posts, would be an opportunity for peer pressure, bullying, and harassment. But a seventy-four-year-old presidential candidate saw them as a conduit for political messaging.

Bernie Sanders made his Snapchat debut in November of 2015 and immediately drew hordes of followers. Soon people began to customize Bernie’s image using a feature called “geofilters.” In Iowa, you could frame your selfie with a cartoon Bernie holding a match and imploring your followers to “feel the Bern.” In New Hampshire, you could straddle the top of his campaign bus like a steer, and ride through the White Mountains.

And so, voila: Bernie Sanders had become a meme, which, as the film scholar Nico Baumbach has noted, is a “sameness machine” (related to même, the French word for “same”) that also works as a “difference machine.” Internet memes mutate by superimposing onto a standard template whatever is weird, funny, wild, or otherwise hyper-specific. You can make an overweight cat ask, for example, “I can haz cheeseburger?” or make Sanders, exasperated and wearing an enormous parka, declare “I am once again asking” for, well, fill in the blanks: for your kid not to pee on the toilet seat, for your girlfriend to marry you, for tonight to be taco night.

But in Vermont, Sanders was a meme before the Internet came along. Soon after his political career began in 1970, newspapers started using a kind of shorthand to describe him: the “disheveled,” “bombastic,” “radical,” “perennial candidate,” who always “railed against” a predictable battery of targets: banks, oil companies and, yes, billionaires. In those days of grassroots campaigning, Sanders turned up in each new rec hall and beer tent, always immutably himself: same booming Brooklyn voice, same all-in physicality, same motheaten sweater, same shitkickers. The sameness made him different: different from his rural, taciturn constituents, and different from any politician that those voters had met, or even imagined. But it was, everywhere, the same difference: whether in Pownal or Peacham or Putney, voters saw the guy and heard the pitch, season after season.

The image spread (we could say “went viral”) in two linked, old-fashioned ways: there emerged a word-of-mouth corpus of Bernie hitchhiking stories. Sanders could be recognized, of course, even as you whizzed past him on the highway, and if you slowed down to pick him up, you were treated at very close range to the same message that has now, many decades down the road, galvanized crowds and changed American politics. It was around this time that Sanders entered the Vermont imaginary more or less in his current form: realizing Bernard Sanders’s inevitable likeness to himself, Vermonters, comparing notes, rechristened him “Bernie.” The effect had important comic potential from the start: it would be just a matter of time before Bernie turned up at Leonardo’s The Last Supper or at a bachelorette party at Sea World.

His frazzled presence seems a weird fit for the feed, but from the beginning of his public life, Sanders was an impresario of emergent media. Researching Bernie for Burlington, my book on Sanders’s rise, I found I could tag my protagonist, like a deer or a shark, as he popped up in successive communications habitats. He began as the house harangue-writer for Vermont’s first statewide alternative paper, The Vermont Freeman, delivered by VW Bus to gas stations and A & P’s along the new interstates. The writing was terrible, but the voice was indelible. Soon Bernie published and edited his own newsletter, Movement, distributing it from his backpack. When Sanders moved to Burlington in 1971, he immediately located the AV room of the Fletcher Free Library and began to fiddle around. In the late Seventies he peddled a series of homemade historical filmstrips on local and leftist politics to village schools and libraries, and produced documentaries for distribution on Vermont’s nascent ETV networks, seizing the local boards and forcing them to preempt somnambulant fare like I, Claudius and Upstairs, Downstairs.

Then as now, there was a friable line between what counted as “virtual” and what defined “real life.” Campaigning for mayor of Burlington in 1981, Sanders distributed meaty, durable shopping bags to the elderly, emblazoned on both sides with campaign slogans. Images of old ladies fording snow-caked sidewalks to get to far-flung pharmacies with their “Bernie Bags” made it to the news, and dramatized the city’s loss of neighborhood services. In 1985 Sanders supported, and then coopted, Burlington’s new public access channel, CCTV. This got him out of City Hall and back onto the streets: as a teenager in town, I met him for the first time. As the host of “Bernie Speaks: The Mayor’s Show,” Bernie interviewed skate punks, walleye fishermen, and my cousins, ice skating on Lake Champlain. When it came time to reintroduce himself to the state as a candidate for US Congress in 1988, Sanders peddled his gospel cassette, We Shall Overcome, to local radio. It was bad; it was great; it was different; but it was, as people had started to say, not just Bernie but “very Bernie.”

Advertisement

In a sameness so profoundly realized that it becomes a difference, we see the customizable formula that has fed dozens of outsider campaigns across America, and promises to inspire more. Zohran Mamdani’s campaign for mayor of New York City used Bernie’s Burlington campaigns as its blueprint; Zohran remained Zohran, down to the trim black suit, whether snuggling a bodega cat or joining a Sikh Nagar Kirtan. It was comical, it was moving; most of all, it was what we mean by “authentic,” a refusal to curtail one’s convictions to the pressures of the moment.

The sameness is often indicated by dress, but it is not mere style. It’s in a message that only intensifies when it detects the impetus toward moderation. Some New Yorkers were offended by their mayor’s expression of condolence on October 7, the third anniversary of the Hamas attacks on Israeli civilians, since it also mourned the 74,000 or more Palestinians who have perished in the Israeli genocide. In Michigan, Dr. Abdul El-Sayed has worn the same black, gym-bro v-neck t-shirt to many of his stops, where his message, too, has been uniform: money in your pocket, money out of politics, Medicare for all. During a 2026 floor protest in the Florida legislature, Angie Nixon, now an upstart candidate for US Senate, delivered her anti-redistricting message through hot-pink bullhorn. When the action drew a harsh Republican reprimand, Nixon saw a fast lane: it appears from polling that Nixon, a Black socialist, could conceivably win in a state that Donald Trump carried in 2024 by 13 points.

All of these candidates establish as definitive their differences not from Republicans, who, since they are beneath contempt, are mostly beyond mentioning; but instead from mainstream Democrats, and they mark that difference by refusing most PAC money. El-Sayed withstood a barrage of some $30 million in campaign contributions to his rival from AIPAC, the American Israel Public Affairs Committee. The deficit became a symbol for his authenticity, his difference.

Sanders, meanwhile, has been criss-crossing the nation supporting these candidates who see it his way, who share his vision. That is sometimes, mercifully, where the similarities end. To see him on stage with a young Black legislator, or an Egyptian American doctor, or a Uganda-born South Asian mayor, is to note the value, for Bernie Sanders, of difference. The knock on Bernie has always been that he hails from one of the two whitest states in the Union, and one of the most progressive. Vermont, it is said, is something like Sweden. How could such a figure scale his appeal nationally? The answer has been to cultivate sameness, but embrace difference. It seems like a different difference this time around.

entries.title: America’s Second Gilded Age
entries.summary: Season 1, Episode 3 of Endgame with Fintan O’Toole
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
In the third episode of Endgame with Fintan O’Toole, the historian Jean Strouse discusses the parallels between our current American moment and the Gilded Age. She and O’Toole talk about the roots of our modern American institutions in the Gilded Age, when the country’s business leaders imported cultural as well as financial capital, and relied greatly on migration. Looking at the origins of figures like J. Pierpont Morgan and Levi Strauss, Strouse examines how a kind of enlightened self-interest motivated the robber barons and industrial capitalists who set the course for much of the American twentieth century.

Jean Strouse is the author, most recently, of Family Romance: John Singer Sargent and the Wertheimers—about the painter’s relationship to the family of Asher Wertheimer, a London art dealer who commissioned portraits of himself, his wife, and all ten of their children—as well as biographies of Alice James and J. Pierpont Morgan. She has written for the Review on subjects that range from Henry James to Sargent portraits to a late-in-life romance between Morgan and Lady Victoria Sackville to the Transatlantic cable. Strouse was the director of The New York Public Library’s Cullman Center for Scholars and Writers from 2003 to 2017, and began her career at The New York Review of Books, where she worked as an editorial assistant to Robert Silvers right after graduating from Radcliffe College.

entries.title: Trump’s Blob
entries.summary: In mid-March Sebastian Gorka, the White House’s senior director for counterterrorism, took the stage at the Council on Foreign Relations in Washington, D.C. entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
In mid-March Sebastian Gorka, the White House’s senior director for counterterrorism, took the stage at the Council on Foreign Relations in Washington, D.C. The think tank has served as the inner sanctum of the foreign policy establishment for more than a century: the place where a bipartisan collection of diplomats and strategists planned much of the postwar international order, and where Henry Kissinger published his first bestseller. Throughout its history the Council has prided itself on the collegial tone of its gatherings; its meeting guidelines state that “all participants are expected to maintain the highest levels of civility and respect.” And yet here was Gorka, a MAGA diehard known for threatening journalists and disparaging Islam, discussing the administration’s counterterrorism strategy with the PBS correspondent Nick Schifrin.

Gorka started by attacking Joe Kent, the head of the National Counterterrorism Center, who had just resigned from the Trump administration over the 2026 Iran war, calling him “an utter disgrace.” He lavished praise upon Trump (“What the president has done is absolutely astounding”) and insulted the press, from “the scum at Politico” to the “HuffPo jokers” to a New York Times journalist whom he described as “some piece of human filth.” He grew more combative as the conversation progressed, taking an errant swipe at the “transgender lunacy flag,” dressing down a Harvard Law School lecturer who tried to question him about Congress’s constitutionally granted war powers—“Who’s the commander in chief?” Gorka repeatedly asked—and lashing out when asked whether the administration planned for blowback from Iran: “I mean, you have to be smoking Hunter Biden’s crack pipe to believe this crap.” In each case, the moderator moved on to the next question.

Though Gorka exuded confidence on the CFR dais, he was in fact largely unwelcome in most policy circles until recently. During the first Trump term, he lasted less than a year in the White House, and was unable to obtain a security clearance; Foreign Policy denounced him as a “far-right nativist” and a “terrible scholar,” and even John Bolton called him a “con man.” Between Trump’s terms, he hosted a radio show called America First, entirely shut out of the mainstream save for appearances on Fox News.

But since Trump returned to office, the bipartisan foreign policy establishment has seemed eager to bring figures like Gorka into the fold. CFR recently hired Trump’s former Ukraine envoy Keith Kellogg and economic adviser Pierre Yared as fellows, and has given a stage to more than a dozen second-term officials, including Jamieson Greer, Peter Navarro, Chris Wright, Doug Burgum, and Elbridge Colby. (Kristi Noem, then Homeland Security secretary, was due to speak in October 2025 but canceled two days before.) The Atlantic Council has brought on at least eight Trump administration alumni, including the former homeland security adviser Julia Nesheiwat (recently nominated for an ambassadorship-at-large to the Arctic), who sits on its board as well as being a distinguished fellow. The Center for a New American Security (CNAS), founded in 2007 to give the Democratic Party stronger defense bona fides in the George W. Bush era, now hosts events with Trump officials, like the hostage envoy Adam Boehler, who headlined the opener of its National Security Exchange series in September 2025; CNAS retains Ellen Lord, formerly the Trump Pentagon’s top weapons buyer, on its board of advisers. Not every institution has this access: at a January 2026 trade event, the Brookings Institution’s economic studies director said that “multiple” administration officials had been invited and none accepted.

The pattern continues beyond Washington. Sean Spicer and Corey Lewandowski have been fellows at the Harvard Institute of Politics, and Mick Mulvaney and Ken Cuccinelli at the University of Chicago Institute of Politics. Robert O’Brien, Trump’s national security adviser during the January 6 attack on the Capitol, was in the first class of distinguished fellows at the Columbia University Institute of Global Politics. Trump’s former National Security Council chief of staff Fred Fleitz, of the America First Policy Institute, spoke at London’s Chatham House in early October.

This courtship hasn’t abated since the Pentagon suspended engagement with think tanks in 2025, starting with its abrupt withdrawal from the Aspen Institute’s annual security forum on the grounds that the meeting, in the words of a Pentagon spokesperson, “promotes the evil of globalism, disdain for our great country, and hatred for the President of the United States.” (Aspen, in typically bipartisan fashion, continues to send invitations to Trump officials.) Senior officials at lower-profile agencies—such as Greer, the administration’s trade representative—still visit mainstream think tanks in D.C., which have also hosted off-the-record sessions with appointees like United Nations Ambassador Mike Waltz. And the ban itself has sometimes proven porous, as when Pete Hegseth spoke at the Reagan National Defense Forum, a traditional Republican conference, in December.

Advertisement

Even when MAGA figures aren’t present, establishment gatherings increasingly seem to echo their brash and pugilistic foreign policy. At the recent Aspen Security Forum, former officials from other administrations treated the interventions of Trump’s second term—the overthrow of Venezuela’s president without a plan, the initiation of a cataclysmic war on Iran—as an opportunity to imagine how a more conventional presidency might carry on with such bellicosity. “We have big decisions,” Nicholas Burns, a distinguished career diplomat who served as Joe Biden’s ambassador to China and George W. Bush’s to NATO, said at a session on the Western Hemisphere. “Do we intervene in Cuba? Do we intervene in Venezuela further?” Later, former secretary of state Condoleezza Rice championed Trump’s Iran offensive in terms that reprised Bush-era admonitions about the necessity of preemptive war. “People will say the threat wasn’t imminent,” she said. “Do you really want to wait until it’s imminent?”*

Does all this suggest that the establishment is absorbing the tenets of MAGA, translating them into its own idiom? Or has the reverse occurred, with the notoriously hawkish foreign policy elite—what the former Barack Obama adviser Ben Rhodes famously called “the Blob”—tutoring a president who ran as an antiwar candidate in its commitment to militarism? I’m both an observer and a participant in the foreign policy community (I direct a think tank program, spent about a decade as a journalist in Washington, and am a dues-paying term member of the Council), and I’ve been mulling that question as I make the rounds at on- and off-the-record sessions, over lavish luncheon buffets and well-stocked open bars, in Washington and New York.

I’ve been around long enough to recognize that there is nothing novel in the imperialist rhetoric of a military-intervention-first foreign policy; Trump’s Washington sounds a lot like the D.C. of the Bush era. Indeed, the current merger owes much to the fact that the hawks inside and around MAGA—Marco Rubio, Hegseth, the late Senator Lindsey Graham—won the argument against the America First faction that wanted out of the Middle East, a fight that Kent’s resignation made public. But something new does seem to be happening. Bush’s advisers—Rice, Colin Powell, Stephen Hadley, Paul Wolfowitz—were drawn from universities, conservative think tanks, and earlier Republican administrations, with decades of government service between them. Trump’s heavyweights more often arrive from real estate (Steve Witkoff, Jared Kushner), cable news (Hegseth, Gorka), or Silicon Valley (Jacob Helberg), their standing derived from loyalty or private fortune.

And while inviting such people to speak at policy shops is not improper in itself—engaging the government of the day is what these institutions exist to do—it’s worth noting who appears less often than they used to: the career ambassadors, regional specialists, and arms-control negotiators who were once the default speakers, along with the ground-up voices from Palestine, Iran, or Venezuela that were always scarce and are now nearly absent. At the institutions that certify foreign policy expertise, in other words—much as in the White House and the cabinet—MAGA operatives seem to be displacing the traditional diplomatic corps.

Although the Blob only got its name in 2016, an elite, bipartisan clique has been at the center of US foreign policymaking since the beginning of the cold war. In his book Tomorrow, the World (2020), the historian Stephen Wertheim details how a cohort of scholars, planners, and lawyers who came together during World War II designed the global institutions that emerged afterward. Crucially, this group had positions external to government—they were based in places like the Council as well as white-shoe law firms, foundations, and universities—which meant that they persisted from one administration to the next, revolving in and out of jobs in the national security state. From the first, their bias was toward war and military dominance. In the eighteen months between the fall of France and Pearl Harbor, “foreign policy elites undertook a thoroughgoing reevaluation of America’s world role, ultimately concluding that the United States should underwrite international order by securing its own political and military supremacy,” Wertheim writes. They found in the British Empire “a ready-made model for covering the stark coercion of superior force with the veneer of liberal freedom.”

The rarefied world of international affairs has long been siloed from domestic policy; in the postwar period as today, national security leaders were “responsible for the country but not responsive to it,” as David Halberstam wrote in 1972. Even the most disastrous results of American interventionism have never disqualified its proponents from holding senior positions in government. The members of Reagan’s national security team, who allied with paramilitaries that participated in massacres in Central America and mired themselves in scandals like Iran-Contra, continued to find jobs in subsequent administrations. The “peace dividend,” as George H. W. Bush and Margaret Thatcher termed the promise that profuse weapons spending would be redirected after the Berlin Wall fell, never arrived; military budgets just kept growing. Under Bill Clinton, the US bombed Iraq and ensured that the military alliance NATO kept expanding even after the Soviet Union disbanded. During George W. Bush’s presidency, nearly all of Washington rallied behind the expansive and expensive counterterrorism wars, and the Blob never held anyone accountable for the resulting quagmires.

Advertisement

Rhodes, who worked under Obama as his foreign policy speechwriter and deputy national security adviser, coined the term “the Blob” in response to the concerted campaign to stymie the Iran nuclear deal. Swept into office by Obama’s idealistic vision for the world and his ambitious campaign commitment to end the Iraq War, the team that included Rhodes was surprised to learn that “it was harder to build support for a diplomatic agreement with Iran than it was to take our country to war in Iraq,” as Rhodes said in a 2022 podcast interview. The groupthink they encountered was “often reflexively interventionist, without necessarily considering the consequences of interventions.”

In that interview Rhodes described the Blob as an assemblage of policymakers who “overstated the capacity of the United States to shape events inside of other countries, particularly in the Middle East.” The term captured not only the establishment’s tendency to speak in a single voice but also the way it seemingly could not be displaced; whatever blows reality delivered to its worldview, it would spring back into its accustomed shape. As if to affirm the existence of the phenomenon, many of the people who advocated for the Libya overthrow under Obama—which failed on its own terms, leading to civil war—then landed jobs in the Biden administration.

The concept of the Blob, as the name might also imply, is slippery and hard to pin down, not quite an ideology or a network or a collection of specific institutions but rather a combination of the three. The term irked many members of the establishment. “It’s a pejorative and imprecise way to dismiss those who disagree with you, and it doesn’t advance the foreign policy conversation,” Richard Haass, then the president of the Council on Foreign Relations, told The New York Times in 2021. Others, like the former CIA director and career ambassador William Burns, have embraced the moniker in their own writing. Some have gone so far as to praise the group it describes. “In truth, the foreign policy establishment is an American strength rather than weakness,” the conservative academics Hal Brands, Peter Feaver, and William Inboden wrote in Foreign Affairs in 2020, in an article titled “In Defense of the Blob.” “It is more open-minded and accountable than its critics allow. It acts as a storehouse of accumulated professional wisdom, providing intellectual ballast to the ship of state.”

When it comes to mapping the Blob, certain think tanks are helpful landmarks, though it might be more accurate to focus on individuals, who often wear multiple hats at various institutions (working as lobbyists and consultants; serving on the boards of defense contractors and, recently, tech companies; and burnishing their CVs with think tank fellowships and scholarly sinecures). In short, the Blob is made up of influential people without a constituency. Membership is less about particular pedigrees or positions than an almost religious belief in American exceptionalism and a fervent commitment to a mode of postwar imperialism in which the United States’ status as an empire is never explicitly acknowledged.

The Blob largely rejected Trump in 2016. In an open letter that March, 122 Republican national security experts called him “utterly unfitted to the office.” This hostility surely had something to do with Trump’s call to “drain the swamp,” of which the Blob was clearly a part. But many leading voices of the establishment also misunderstood the president as an isolationist. “It is revealing that his adopted slogan of ‘America First’ initially gained currency in the 1930s as the isolationist banner of Charles Lindbergh, who fought to keep the US out of the fight against Hitler’s Germany,” Haass wrote in the Wall Street Journal in 2016, warning that “the consequences of a lasting American retreat from the world would be dire.”

A few traditional Republican figures—Bolton and Mike Pompeo, as well as many nonpartisan military and intelligence officers—joined the new administration as national security cabinet members and senior advisers. They saw themselves as being there to keep an unconventional leader in check; the press dubbed them “the axis of adults,” a label Bolton referenced in his memoir The Room Where It Happened. (Bolton later warned, in a 2024 foreword to the book, that “Mr. Trump’s most dangerous legacy is the spread of the isolationist virus in the Republican Party.”)

Before long, however, Trump started displaying a penchant for interventionism. In 2017 he dropped the so-called Mother of All Bombs—the most powerful nonnuclear explosive in America’s arsenal—on Islamic State fighters in Afghanistan; he also accelerated drone strikes on Somalia and Yemen by relaxing the rules of engagement. In January 2020 he ordered a strike on the Iranian commander Qasem Suleimani. Some in the Blob hailed such moves as bold expressions of American power: in April 2017, after Trump launched dozens of Tomahawk missiles on Syria, Antony Blinken, later Biden’s secretary of state, wrote that Trump “was right to strike.” CNN’s Fareed Zakaria declared, “I think Donald Trump became president of the United States last night.”

With Trump’s loss to Biden in 2020, it became difficult for former Trump appointees to get jobs at establishment institutions, except for a handful of experts with the right credentials. Yet MAGA insiders still found affiliations at traditional neocon redoubts, like the Hoover Institution at Stanford, the Hudson Institute, and the Foundation for Defense of Democracies. The influx of Trump alums into these Blob strongholds was part of a broader trend in which conservative organizations started taking on a more Trumpian feel; MAGA even took over the Heritage Foundation by 2021. At the same time, MAGA types created their own institutions, like the America First Policy Institute, which hosted cabinet officials and developed ideas in tandem with Project 2025, and the Abraham Accords Peace Institute, which focused on Middle East policy (and has since been integrated into Heritage).

As the Trump-aligned wing of the Republican Party gained importance, establishment figures began more openly cultivating relationships with their MAGA counterparts. In 2023 Hillary Clinton cofounded the Institute of Global Politics at Columbia University, which invited prominent practitioners as visiting scholars; it soon brought on Pompeo, who had served as Trump’s secretary of state and CIA director during his first term, as a fellow. Pompeo had laid a variety of traps to sabotage the incoming Biden administration, redesignating the Houthis as a terrorist group and upgrading relations with Taiwan. As secretary of state, he had threatened to release Clinton’s emails; earlier, when he was a member of Congress, he grilled her over the Benghazi affair. But last November they appeared together on stage at Columbia’s School of International and Public Affairs in New York. After Clinton described the perceived threat from China in stark terms—saying that “the principal problem” for the US is whether it or “the Chinese Communist Party model” is “going to succeed in the twenty-first century”—Pompeo replied, “I agree with almost everything Secretary Clinton said there.”

Clinton nodded. “Record that,” she said.

By then the Blob had embraced major aspects of Trump’s foreign policy as its preferred solutions to long-held problems. In the Middle East, Washington’s think tanks prioritized establishing diplomatic relations between Israel and the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, in a continuation of the normalization pacts Trump had sealed, known as the Abraham Accords—effectively putting aside the question of a Palestinian state. Biden never rejoined the nuclear deal with Iran, from which Trump had withdrawn, and never fully resumed the operations of the US embassy in Cuba.

Perhaps most notably, Biden’s administration more or less adopted the hawkish approach to China that the Trump team had laid out in its National Security Strategy in 2017. (Though the Trump plan built, to a certain extent, on Obama’s “Pivot to Asia,” it intensified the prior administration’s focus on “strategic competition,” defined as economic and geopolitical rivalry between two great powers, in the distinctly militarized terms that have since won over Washington.) “The best area so far of President Biden’s foreign policy has been on China,” Matthew Pottinger, Trump’s first-term deputy national security adviser and architect of his team’s Asia policy, said on CFR’s podcast The President’s Inbox. “It’s been a policy of continuity in many respects; he’s not dialed back many of the significant steps that we took during the Trump administration.”

Though he ran for a second term as an antiwar candidate—promising to end the Ukraine war on Day One and arrive with the Gaza cease-fire that Biden had failed to secure—Trump made it clear almost as soon as he retook office that he would in fact spend his term exerting military power. Within a year, he had launched extrajudicial strikes on boats that have since killed more than two hundred people in the Caribbean and the Pacific, in what legal scholars say amounts to murder. Some members of the Blob have noted the clear illegality of the strikes, while others, like Elliott Abrams, Trump’s first-term Venezuela and Iran envoy, argued in the fall of 2025 that they should go even further. Graham said that Trump had “all the authority in the world.”

There is plenty of precedent, of course, for the Blob cheering as an administration runs roughshod over US and international law. But the foreign policy establishment has tended to couch its interventionism in altruistic terms. The Trump administration, in contrast, doesn’t talk about winning hearts and minds or carrying liberties to unfree quarters of the globe; this is about raw American power, an attitude exemplified by the Jerusalem cross—the emblem of the Crusades—tattooed on Hegseth’s chest. As the president posted on Truth Social in April, “with a little more time, we can easily OPEN THE HORMUZ STRAIT, TAKE THE OIL, & MAKE A FORTUNE.”

And yet when Trump first waged war on Iran in June 2025, joining Israel in twelve days of hostilities, even Democratic hawks couldn’t entirely condemn the maneuver. As Blinken wrote in The New York Times, “The strike on three of Iran’s nuclear facilities by the United States was unwise and unnecessary. Now that it’s done, I very much hope it succeeded.” Earlier that month, when the US was engaged in diplomacy with Iran over its nuclear program, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer used the acronym “TACO”—for “Trump Always Chickens Out”—in a social media post that mocked the president for holding off on military intervention.

The overthrow of Venezuela’s president, Nicolás Maduro, further invigorated the Blob. Both Republicans and Democrats have pursued devastating economic sanctions against the country for nearly two decades. While many from the Democratic establishment criticized Trump’s disregard for international law when news broke of the kidnapping, they also evinced a certain awe. “When we saw this operation unfold and we heard the results of it, I think we all thought, damn, that’s impressive,” Jake Sullivan, Biden’s national security adviser, said on the podcast he cohosts, The Long Game.

The Blob, then, decries Trump’s disregard for norms while admiring the results of his lawlessness. Asked at Aspen about the worst part of Trump’s second term so far, Hadley said, “I think they need more process, they need more discipline.” After Maduro’s kidnapping, the lawmakers who criticized the president likewise did so mostly on proceduralist grounds, arguing that he should have sought congressional authorization for the coup. But the Democratic leadership hardly mounted resistance even amid signs that another US attack—on Iran, or possibly Cuba—was imminent. The former Republican Representative Marjorie Taylor Greene, an America First hardliner, objected in stronger terms than Democrats in Congress: “The ‘peace president’ went to war and is killing and wounding our troops,” she posted about Iran in June 2026.

These feeble responses from outside the administration have found an echo in the striking lack of dissent within it, beyond a handful of resignations like Kent’s. Since retaking office Trump has presided over the transformation of the security state. In his first term, he struggled to implement his foreign policy platform because of bureaucratic incompetence, internal resistance, and a muddled strategy. Over the past two years, his administration has systematically remade departments and agencies: Elon Musk dismantled USAID, Trump confidants purged the State Department’s career officers and other bureaucrats across government, and Hegseth transformed the Department of Defense into a “Department of War.” The civil servants who managed to hang on to jobs have largely accepted the current political climate and decided not to take the risk of pushing back. That has had broader effects, as the academic and former Obama administration defense policy adviser Van Jackson argued in his Substack newsletter, Un-Diplomatic. “My sense is that a large portion of people working in government right now are numb to just how far-right the state apparatus itself has become,” he wrote. “The Blob, in other words, is part MAGA now and scarcely realizes it.”

The foreign policy establishment is also being shaped by its relationship with a new, and newly influential, military tech sector. The Council has invited executives from Peter Thiel’s Palantir to speak about defense innovation and the ever-popular topic of AI, and held sessions with executives from Anduril—the military tech mega-startup founded by the MAGA billionaire Palmer Luckey—and the Trump-aligned venture capital behemoth Andreessen Horowitz. While the Blob has always included figures with close ties to the “primes”—the leading legacy defense firms—the new military tech mavens are arriving in Washington with a decidedly partisan political project. Companies like Musk’s SpaceXAI and Thiel’s Palantir have deep ties to MAGA, from Musk serving on the new Project Meridian commission to Thiel’s mentees serving throughout the executive branch. As they’ve gained power and authority, however, national security leaders from the Biden administration have also begun to pass through the revolving door to work for them, or for companies in the related finance sector. Biden officials have joined investment firms that partner with Musk and Thiel’s outfits, or been hired by Anduril or Andreessen Horowitz.

Jacob Helberg, a top Trump State Department official responsible for economic diplomacy, lately of Palantir, spoke in April at the Council’s Washington office about replacing traditional foreign assistance with investment and commercial diplomacy. During the Q&A, I asked whether anti-American sentiment—in response to the vast number of civilians killed in Iran and the US’s provision of weapons for what many have described as a genocide in Gaza—was impeding his diplomatic entreaties. The answer came in business terms. “Well, the Philippines just gifted us unconditionally 4,000 acres” for a high-tech industrial park, Helberg replied. “So I think it’s going pretty well. We’re not seeing any slowdown in interest or in desire to partner with the United States.” I heard similar language at other prominent think tanks. In April the deputy secretary of state, Christopher Landau, speaking at the Atlantic Council’s Global Prosperity Forum, said: “It’d be amazing to think of an Iran that was not an enemy state, but a state that would welcome private sector investment from the US and other countries.”

One reason that establishment institutions have increasingly welcomed the MAGA set may be that the latter promises to fill a vacuum of ideas at the former. The foreign policy consensus about the Middle East is a case in point. The think tanks were clearly at a loss after the attacks of October 7, 2023. In the weeks and months that followed, they largely avoided acknowledging the human cost of Israel’s military campaigns across the region—or even discussing the risk of blowback or legal liability for US policymakers. I went to homepage after homepage looking for analyses of Israeli war crimes and how they were damaging American interests, and found almost nothing. By fall of 2025, my organization’s polling showed that a third of Americans viewed Israel’s actions in Gaza as a genocide, and other polls suggest it may now be closer to four in ten. But the think tanks never mobilized the way they did at the start of the Ukraine war, when they spotlighted Russian atrocities.

Instead of hosting its own discussions about Israel and Palestine, the Blob seems to be signing onto Trump’s disruptive proposals. After decades in which the traditional goal of a two-state solution has come to seem increasingly far-fetched, institutions like the Middle East Institute or the Atlantic Council have appeared energized by the normalization agreements between Israel and Arab states. In 2025 the Middle East Institute brought on Kenneth Pollack, an influential advocate of the Iraq War, as vice president for studies; it also parted ways with Khaled Elgindy, who directed its Palestine program. Events on Israel–Palestine have dwindled, and judging by their descriptions, Israeli normalization comes up roughly twice as often as Palestinian statehood.

A similar phenomenon is playing out at other institutions. At a recent Atlantic Council event, the moderator, the longtime Middle East hand Brett McGurk, asked Syrian president Ahmed al-Sharaa about the prospect of establishing diplomatic ties to Israel without mentioning the long-standing prerequisite of creating a Palestinian state. The Trump formulation for Middle East policy, however contested, has become Washington’s status quo.

In a June article for the Financial Times, Hillary Clinton defended the president’s Board of Peace, a multilateral organization with pay-to-play membership requirements that appointed Trump—as an individual, not as the US president—to serve as its chairman, seemingly for life. (The human rights attorney Zaha Hassan has warned that the lack of oversight makes the board highly susceptible to corruption, and noted that it plans to “forcibly displace and dispossess Palestinians.”) Clinton presented her support as a matter of pragmatism, despite the fact that the board has done little to alleviate the humanitarian catastrophe in Gaza. “The Board of Peace and the plan contain elements many governments dislike or disagree with,” she wrote. “Yet if even I, an implacable opponent of the president, can accept that this is the best option, then surely others can too?”

This is the kind of alliance that Pompeo touted earlier this year at the JPMorganChase Center for Geopolitics. Its director, Derek Chollet, worked as a senior Biden national security official and one of Blinken’s closest advisers. Formerly a critic of Pompeo’s tenure in the cabinet, Chollet hosted him in February on the center’s podcast to discuss leadership. “We’re going to be just fine,” Pompeo said, “if we can get our senior leaders to sort of figure this all out and stop shouting and start talking.”

entries.title: A Collective Reminiscing

entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
Over the course of the 1970s and early 1980s, Theresa Hak Kyung Cha created a small body of art and writing celebrated in Asian American culture for its embrace of difficulty. Her best-known project, the experimental text Dictee (1982), contains an unpredictable mix of forms—catechism, letter, biography, schoolbook—and images ranging from anatomy charts and Paleolithic cave art to brush calligraphy by Cha’s father. Its title alludes to French dictation exercises, and near the start it uses those exercises as a poetic structure:

Open paragraph It was the first day period She had come from a far period tonight at dinner comma the families would ask comma open quotation marks How was the first day interrogation mark close quotation marks at least to say the least of it possible comma the answer would be open quotation marks there is but one thing period There is someone period From a far period close quotation marks

Her video installations and performances are just as demanding, often erasing context in a bid to force the viewer into perceiving the familiar with new eyes. One untitled Super 8 work runs the camera over everyday objects, such as an umbrella’s spokes, in unrecognizably close detail. In another, phrases such as “far, “farther,” and “far again” flash across a white screen at irregular intervals. One of her more elaborate mature projects, Exilée (1980), sets a small cathode-ray television within a larger, wall-sized projection; the two channels play contrasting, apparently unrelated scenes while a recording of Cha’s breathy, flutelike voice reads peculiar selections from what sounds like corporate mail, a Japanese menu, and a poem about time zones.

Recurring fixations emerge across her work: language’s quirks and failures, the play of black and white, scenes from early childhood, an intense love of family, French culture, Korean history. Cha came of age as an artist in the heyday of structuralist and psychoanalytic theory, which honed her efforts to break open symbols and probe preconscious states. Rejecting conventional sense-making posed a particular challenge in an era when American audiences often expected Asian artists and writers to offer straightforward, ethnography-like representations of their “home cultures.”

Her output has inspired a tradition of experiment, especially among women artists of Korea’s diaspora. More than a generation of poets—among them Myung Mi Kim, Cathy Park Hong, Don Mee Choi, and Monica Youn—have named her as an influence, as have visual and performance artists including Mandy El-Sayegh, Renée Green, Na Mira, and Latipa. In The New York Times’s “Overlooked No More” series, the novelist Min Jin Lee recalls reading Cha for the first time and admiring her “sense of entitlement to have that level of difficulty.” In the literary critic Rachel Carroll’s eyes, “Cha has accrued an increasingly large and rhapsodic following, exactly because of her difficulty, in form and content, and not despite it.”1

But Cha’s archives attest to a surprising second voice: clearer, angrier, self-possessed. Among her papers is a letter written in capitals on the back of a program to the photographer Richard Barnes, then her fiancé, in which she fumes over how the Women’s Caucus for Art invited her to participate in an SFMOMA group show, but then left her no time to rehearse Exilée properly: “The room is totally light, the wall is not built, nothing is ready. I am ready. Wasting my time,” she wrote. “They act as though they are doing us a favor, rather, we are merely janitors. We are being used to promote themselves, and they are using their female sex, titling themselves feminists…and using other women for their own status quo.” She leaves implied that her heritage in what was then the developing world looked good on the group’s promotional materials.

Cha was then about to turn thirty. When she was eleven, her family left Korea following Park Chung Hee’s military coup. She moved to the Bay Area by fourteen, and spent much of her adult life there. Her invitation to the SFMOMA performance came when she was three years out of an MFA at UC Berkeley and living in New York, where she worked as an assistant at the Met and a video art instructor at a Yonkers college. Her art was on the brink of wider recognition, especially in San Francisco. She had shown in Paris, Amsterdam, Melbourne, and Reykjavik, and hungered for more—including larger audiences, even when she didn’t want to make it easy for them. She held high standards for finish and polish, including in work that can feel improvisatory. Her letter continues, “If it’s not ready, I will not show, and I will use my microphone to announce why, I will practice my speech in examining this entire oppressive situation.” Her obliquity grew from a perfectly clear sense of purpose. For whom was she cultivating it?

Advertisement

Cha’s career ended less than two years after she wrote that frustrated note. A serial rapist assaulted and murdered her in New York in November 1982. Every writer on Cha feels obligated to strike a difficult balance between two imperatives: not to let her violent death eclipse her work, but also not to euphemize racialized sexual violence. Her reputation never waned; her friends, family, and colleagues faithfully tended her legacy. But pursuing a murder conviction required three exhausting, preoccupying trials, which dragged on till the end of 1987. By the early 1990s, when an Association of Asian American Studies panel on Dictee led to the first book-length study on Cha, Writing Self, Writing Nation, its five contributors tended to speak as if they were recovering an overlooked figure—a woman artist of color whose work deserved and repaid the kind of line-by-line attention long trained on writers such as Joyce or Nabokov.

“Multiple Offerings,” the largest retrospective of Cha’s work to date, debuted at the Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive before starting its current run at New York’s Artists Space. The exhibit’s excellent catalog, edited by Victoria Sung, incorporates a wealth of material not on view and triples the amount of art reproduced in the only previous publication of Cha’s work, an out-of-print black-and-white volume. Dictee has long drawn more attention than Cha’s videos, installations, performances, and films; “Multiple Offerings” makes her scope more fully legible and accessible.

Sung’s ampler curation reveals the consistency of Cha’s voice and themes over time. Her earliest datable student work, a 1973 handmade book titled 坤 Earth (Dedicated to Parents), appears full-fledged:

CALLOUS WEST BITTER HEARTS

LAUGH

CELEBRATE PAIN

SUN CONTEMPTUOUS

SOMEWHERE NAMELESS

IN THICK WALLS

CHANTING AROUND AND AROUND

STRANGE FOREIGN TONGUE

RETREATED.

ROWING DIGGING

RESISTING SPACE NEVER FULL OR LOST

STARING ONE ASKS,

WAS IT A NICE DREAM?

CHANGING FACE

MIRRORS YELLOW

She was still working with many of the same images a decade later: walls, ritual, language, dreams, foreignness. Her sense of exile in an America she found strange and hostile (“callous West, bitter hearts”) recalls childhood memories she often revisited, especially from around 1962, when, as an eleven-year-old living temporarily in Hawai’i, she found herself surrounded by “strange foreign” English. (That experience may be the topic of the “Open paragraph” near Dictee’s beginning.) She later wrote that she wanted to trigger the same experience of prelinguistic thought in her audience, the sense of knowing “the roots of the language before it is born on the tip of the tongue.”

Her Catholic high school in San Francisco taught her French, and that third language constantly ran through her adult mind, weaving polyglot puns. Her intuition that thought exists prior to articulation in a particular language led her to try to impart that feeling to others, to simulate prelinguistic experience not just for monoglots but even across the different experiences of multilingualism within her family. The subtitle is a dedication, but also an address. The work betrays no concern that her parents might find it disorienting, and her mother in particular seems to have treasured everything her daughter made. She published a Korean-language book of her own after her daughter’s death, The Little Black Dot I Left Behind.

Some of Cha’s difficulty seems born of intimacy. Viewing or reading it feels like overhearing a family story or flipping through a photo album, sometimes literally: her 1977 Chronology consists of family pictures subjected to degradation through heavy photocopying, surrounded by mysterious, punning phrases set in mismatched type sizes. “could have b ee n knot one / pa / cing second” hovers below a photo of her mother’s face superimposed over her father’s.

The surfaces in Cha’s art are often sleek, the tactics estranging; the work forces you into a pose of decipherment. But when you see it gathered in one place, it welcomes you into a family-like world. The postcards address you, the videos of even the strangest performances evoke some shared memory, the photographs of sites in Cha’s high school, college, or homes touch you even when the overall work offers little other traction. Cha took great interest in ritual, which appears throughout her work, and recent interpreters have read much of her art as enacting a kind of rite. The exhibit feels at times like a kind of home shrine, a memorial to a departed friend or family member. Some artists have literalized this: the first installment in the performer Dohye Lee’s ARA project (2014–2018) borrowed from Korean folk ritual in a work meant to “bring [Cha’s] spirit back to her home.”

Advertisement

At BAMPFA, “Multiple Offerings” traced a roughly chronological path through Cha’s work, starting from her undergraduate years and continuing through White Dust from Mongolia, an unfinished feature film project; Exilée, projected in a room-size space of its own; and source materials from Dictee at the very end, such as the images from postcards she used in altered form as the work’s ghostly illustrations. Her scale increases, as does the cost of her media. Super 8 gives way to 16mm; stenciled graphite, handmade bookwork, and mail art evolve into Dictee’s two hundred pages. She worked almost entirely in black and white, which makes one piece in color shocking: Display-ce, a carousel of Kodachrome slides depicting envelopes crumpled, stuffed, folded, or labeled, rich visually because of their red inner lining.

The most eye-catching material is her work in film and video, astonishing to those of us who have long had to imagine it from a handful of stills. She appears in many of her moving-image pieces, such as Untitled (Paper), where she waves, folds, and brushes pieces of paper across a table, slightly out of focus. In Translations from a Willow Tree (1976) she walks the camera past the windows of an upper-floor apartment over sans-serif words stenciled on the glass, floating in front of a stately building across the street. The surviving footage from White Dust from Mongolia plays on a loop, revealing the full, strange range of what Cha returned to Korea in 1979–1980 to shoot. Minutes pass watching fairground rides, people walking in and out of markets, slow horizontal pans over tile roofs, alleyways full of charcoal smoke. In contrast with Korean feature films from that period, her images feel like a time capsule stuffed with patient observations of ephemera.

Cha benefited from the support of friends, teachers, and institutions as she trained at making the kinds of art that earn a living slowly, if at all. She spent most of her adult life in degree programs at UC Berkeley: one BA in comparative literature, a second BA in art, then an MA in art, and finally an MFA, studying in Europe on Berkeley grants. Even after she graduated, she supported her work with a postdoctoral fellowship from the university. It was natural for Cha’s surviving family to place her archive with BAMPFA. In its Berkeley showing, “Multiple Offerings” incorporated a small selection of art by Cha’s teachers and friends, many from the Bay Area. Her instructor Jim Melchert, an artist across many media who taught for decades at Berkeley, had a quiet presence through his photographs of performance pieces. Melchert introduced her to the performance artist Terry Fox, also included.

The show also offered room to Cha’s peer circle. A large work on painted fabric by the artist and poet Cecilia Vicuña, who knew Cha in her final New York years through the feminist journal Heresies, towered over the central space in a memorial posture. Reese Williams, whose New York-based independent press, Tanam, published Cha’s print work, appeared briefly; so too did a video work by Yong Soon Min, a fellow Korean artist in America whose career until her death in 2024 offers a glimpse of the longer life Cha, too, might have had. (The three overlapped as students at Berkeley.) “Multiple Offerings” never strays far from Cha herself, but both the exhibit and the catalogue, in essays on Cha’s education by Tausif Noor and on Fox by the Artists Space exhibit organizer Danielle Jackson, do address the question of how to read her work as part of a shared milieu. They portray Cha as an artist who plied many trends of the time at least once—especially performance art and small, vernacular media—but never settled into just one form for long.

The greater share of the BAMPFA exhibition’s ancillary space went to younger artists working under Cha’s influence. Video pieces from the 1990s by Renée Green and L. Franklin Gilliam make clear that artists outside Asian American orbits took early interest in borrowing and imitating gestures and topics of Cha’s: filming oneself holding printed text to suggest the silencing of one’s voice, for instance. Contributions made within the past decade by young, ambitious, transnational Asian artists born in the 1980s illustrate Cha’s electrical attraction. Na Mira’s video installation Marquee recreates many of Cha’s stances on-screen with her own body, to the crackle of Los Angeles-area, Korean-language AM radio; Cici Wu’s Upon Leaving the White Dust projects traces of light from White Dust from Mongolia behind a series of small votive objects corresponding to the film’s storyboard. Jesse Chun works with Korean craft paper, finely slicing asemic language into the surface to produce vertical “concrete poems.” Each finds in Cha a way of pressing language beyond decipherable form—what she called the “tip of the tongue.”

Partly because of the consistency of Cha’s visual style and written voice over time, the work in “Multiple Offerings” often blurs process with product. The voice of her finished, exhibited work is improvisatory, fragmentary, pursuing spontaneous insights or puns. A 1976 work in ink on burlap consists of words including “HAND,” “HEARING,” “HALF MOON,” and “NEARING” intersecting like a crossword, while in Korean script the word dal (“moon”) hovers detached in a corner. Her unpublished notes similarly chase ideas through thickets of quasi-automatic writing until she seizes something:

i have time.

banishment  an insanity  birth to history  past present future

an offering  an erasing  the gum rubber scratching surface of document.

more pressure and more wearing to the tip until paper touches the metal.

an offering. to god the male white beard and flowing white hair robes

yards infinitum seated on a cloud attended by two maiden angels their hair jet black in ropes twisted arches then the rest flowing likewise with wind

This could have been an exercise in verbalizing her memories of Catholic high school, and it reads much the same as—indeed, with less irregular spelling than—passages of finished works such as Photo Essay, a combination of prints with typewritten text:

Yet, the rigid obssessive order

skirts of measured lenths

interdiction of crossed knees, pearl earrings,

patent leather shoes, dances on campus,

frosted hair

single file syncronized gestures:

kneeling, opening and closing desks,

steps down to lunch, cursy.

Elsewhere, however, Cha programs spontaneous-seeming gestures in detail. Untitled (Candle Performance), a twenty-six-minute video work from 1973, records her lighting and then blowing out small plain candles on three tables, as if in a ritual for an unknown religion. The order and timing feel completely arbitrary, but her notes reveal meticulous planning, down to the thirty-fourth shot.

The new exhibit and catalog offer ample selections from grant proposals and production materials that display Cha’s interpretations of her own work in a crisp, blunt idiom closer to her letter about the SFMOMA show than to her voice as artist. She had a clear idea of what she wanted to communicate—but her target was the unconscious and the nonverbal. Réveillé dans la Brume, for instance, a performance piece documented in vivid photos and a punctilious script, aimed to “speculate upon dimensions made visible to us through suggestion…attempting to find some collective key, associations, that would result in a kind of a transformation in the audience, as well as the performer.” Both parts of the title speak to her goal: awakening the viewer from illusion into something higher, yes, but also into a fog or mist rather than immediate clarity.

These documents help reconstruct Cha’s relationship to two aesthetic categories that loom large in her contemporary reception: the difficult and the opaque. In general use, “difficulty” and “opacity” are synonyms. But in the past several decades, they have taken on separate technical meanings in literary and cultural theory. Certain kinds of poetic difficulty, the critic George Steiner wrote in a 1978 essay, “confront us with blank questions about the nature of human speech, about the status of significance, about the necessity and purpose of the construct which we have,” together, “come to perceive as a poem.” He was thinking of how Mallarmé and Celan’s language might resemble Dada or surrealism on the surface—might even be provably indecipherable—and yet were neither mere “nonsense nor planned obfuscation.” More recent critics have used a version of difficulty downstream from Steiner’s as a way into works ranging from William Cowper’s eighteenth-century long poem The Task to the novels of Toni Morrison.

You might think “opacity” would mean something similar, but its meaning runs instead through conversations about race and ethnicity. The Martinican French cultural thinker Édouard Glissant argued in his 1990 book Poétique de la relation for “the right to opacity for everyone” as the opposite of an anthropologizing, missionary “transparency” eager to interpret and explain all cultural difference. In mutual opacity between cultures, one might “feel in solidarity with [the other] or build with him,” but “it is not necessary for me to grasp him.” Opacity has come to describe art designed to be selectively understood by different audiences, and perhaps not understood by certain audiences at all—a form of radical independence, especially from the West’s or a racial majority’s gaze.

Cha’s popularity lies squarely at the intersection of the difficult and the opaque. On the one hand, many viewers and readers identify with her efforts to express the ineffable, as an émigrée whose upbringing left her dislocated among the Korean she spoke as a child, the English she lived in afterward, and the French from her schooling. The German artist Uljana Wolf, mapping Cha’s multilingualism onto her own, writes, “Cha makes traceable what it means to be someone who has a language that is not ‘the right one,’ not their own, not original or real.”

On the other hand, reader after reader over the past quarter century has lionized Cha for using language and image to decline the kind of sense-making the median viewer can decipher, cultivating different degrees of intelligibility for different parts of her audience. Writing in the 2024 collection She Follows No Progression: A Theresa Hak Kyung Cha Reader (edited by Juwon Jun and Rachel Valinsky, staff of the publisher Wendy’s Subway), the literary scholar Jennifer Gayoung Lee credits Dictee with freeing her to ask, “What if I did not want to engage in the exhausting task of making my own personhood as a Korean American woman legible to anglophone readers? Could I choose otherwise?” The sociologist Youbin Kang’s essay in the same volume argues that the violence of “the ways that the dominant misrepresent, thwart and silence the marginalized…runs through Cha’s work and takes expressive form in the illegibility she produces,” in her refusal to defer to “those who hold the gaze: the colonizer, the elite, the capitalist, the male, and the white.”

Yet Cha’s extant statements, lectures, and editorial work all return to the idée fixe of communicating with an abstracted, depersonalized body of viewers and readers, leveraging the particularities of her experiences as a way to deliver them into that preverbal state she prized. Her mail-art piece Audience Distant Relative (1977–1978) consisted of envelopes that she mailed to the gallery each day and invited the audience to open, “as if they were personally addressed to them.” One text generalized her own experience of family separation across the two Koreas into a model for performer and reader:

you are the audience

you are my distant audience

i address you

as i would a distant relative

as if a distant relative

seen only heard only through someone else’s description

neither you nor i

are visible to each other

i can only assume that you can hear me

i can only hope that you hear me

As much of her own life as she poured into her work, she envisioned the autobiographical aspect of her art as only one half of a circuit into which the audience would also put something of themselves. She described her work as a reciprocal covenant, or interfusion: “The artist becoming object for the viewer, the viewer as subject, the artist as subject, and viewer as object.” Her content was often “highly personal, drawn from heritage, memory, et cetera.” But she imagined it creating “a space where the audience are left free to imagine, to remember their own memories… an intimate sharing, a collective experience.” She believed the artist was like a medium trying to locate “some collective key” that would help the viewer unlock the storehouse of shared human memory.

This interest in a shared human unconscious pervades Cha’s work. It emerged from an intellectual and political environment different from our own: Berkeley in the decade after 1968, where Marxism, feminism, and the nascent Asian American movement mixed with psychoanalysis and semiotics. As scholars in the field of Asian American studies frequently recount, it was only in May 1968 that the term “Asian American” entered widespread use, coined by Berkeley student activists in a bid to reject words such as “Oriental” and also unite different ethnic groups under a single banner.

That spring the newly-formed Asian American Political Alliance joined with other racial-minority organizations as a joint Third World Liberation Front to expand the previous year’s call for a Black Studies program into a demand for a Third World College. UC Berkeley called in police to break a strike over the issue in the spring semester of 1969, and created its Department of Ethnic Studies as a compromise measure. By fall the protest’s momentum had diffused, but the university that formed Cha over the next decade continued to grapple with the movement’s vision.

Histories and cultures beyond Europe wanted legitimation from artistic and academic institutions. One strategy was to decenter the West, proposing that thought from the “third world” might be just as central to all humankind as thought from any other location. Against this backdrop, it was reasonable for an ambitious young minority artist to imagine that art drawing on her particular ethnic and racial identity might contribute to the realization of an underlying human identity, might even be essential to it.

Cha took particular interest in Jung, Lacan, and Monique Wittig, all thinkers interested in the idea that myths echo in a shared human mind. For her, that also meant engaging the resources she could find on classical East Asia, scant as they sometimes were in that era: Zhuangzi dreaming about being a butterfly, sixteenth-century Korean poetry. Her early work draws on Korean culture gingerly, in subtle touches—Korean script, Korean religious dance—and both Dictee’s long passages explaining Korea’s history and the surviving materials for White Dust from Mongolia make clear that she drew more confidently on the country as she matured.

She proposed that White Dust from Mongolia would use images of Korea to evoke similar memories in any viewer. “The images and language emerge from sources that are highly personal in that they are accounts from memory, my personal memory as well as the viewer’s memory, therefore, hopefully, a collective reminiscing,” she writes in a funding application. “These given instances in Time attempt as catalysts to evoke other moments in the viewer’s memory.” Dictee places her telling of modern Korean history (then even less known in America than now) next to fragments of cave art, long sequences set in darkrooms and cinemas, and allusions to ancient Greece’s Eleusinian Mysteries.

She seemed to believe in access to a kind of communion through re-narration, or maybe even reincarnation. “Narrative shifts, discovers variation. Each observance prisoner of yet another observance, the illusion of variation hidden in yet another odor yet another shrouding, disguised, superimposed upon,” she muses in Dictee. “Like birth like death. Unlike birth, unlike death, this redeemed through a future and a past through own memory and presumes a separate conclusion.” She imagines herself speaking as a medium for Saint Thérèse of Lisieux, the teenage Korean independence fighter Yu Gwansun, her own mother, and Joan of Arc—her voice giving life to theirs, and their lives giving voice to hers.

Underpinning much of this work was the conviction that one’s own particular cultural heritage could be the portal into a kind of universalism. That vision differs from today’s tendency to prioritize owning one’s culture and fending off potential appropriators. It also differs from Glissant’s emphasis on adopting a style opaque enough to escape the subjugating gaze of others. Cha’s universalism now draws less praise than her uncompromising difficulty. But her interest in Korean particularity as a door to universal relevance suggests that her difficulty served a goal other than opacity. At the very least, her version of visibility was a freely chosen one, not imposed by others’ prying eyes. It was part of a bid for equal dignity, elevating Korea—then still comparatively impoverished—to the same status as a source of pioneering art as New York or Paris. There’s one kind of chutzpah in saying that your art matters more to one community than others. There’s another, equally worthwhile kind in saying that your community’s story is and should be universally relevant and legible, if not easy.

The title “Multiple Offerings” comes from a sentence in the same artist statement where Cha writes about seeking the roots of language: “The focus is in producing Multiple Telling with Multiple Offering.” We normally take the opposite of opacity to be transparency. But Cha’s work suggests an alternative to transparency, with its attendant vulnerability: openness to multiple proliferating audiences across time and place, like the openness of a space filled with people, coming and going. Cha understood herself to be an exile, exilée—rooted in Korea but unable to return, living in America but never comfortable with its culture, fond of Europe but only a visitor there. That sense of exile, I think, laid the foundation for some of her openness to all comers willing to ponder her puzzles. Edward Said once wrote, of the literary critic Erich Auerbach, that great insight comes from exile, quoting the same medieval monk Auerbach often cited: “He is perfect to whom the entire world is as a foreign land.” Everywhere was foreign to Cha, including Korea when she returned to it as an adult. What is remarkable is that in the face of so many displacements, she kept offering so much, and remained open to the tellings she might receive in return.
